passage:
At the batch reunion in a hotel garden, Rekha's startup had a second office and Seema's new husband was pouring the drinks. Hrithik held his glass and smiled at the right moments. On the train home he scrolled through photos of an abroad degree and a house with a balcony that were not his.

That night he made a list. The design course he had skipped because his father said it was not a real degree. The girl he had let go because his family wanted someone from the same town. The year he had spent doing nothing after an exam he had not even wanted to sit. None of those choices had felt like his; each had been settled by somebody else's fear, or by his own.

At home, an aunt asked over tea, "Twenty-five and still no plan? At this age my friend's son had a flat and a wife." A cousin's wedding card sat on the fridge. Hrithik felt time as a sand timer with himself at the bottom of it. Everyone in his community seemed to hold a schedule, and he seemed to have missed the train.

qa.q: What did Rekha's startup have?
qa.a: It had a second office.

qa.q: How did the reunion lead to Hrithik's list and then to his fear of being behind?
qa.a: Seeing Rekha's second office and Seema's new husband made his own path look small. That led him to list the design course, the girl and the wasted year that others' fear had decided, and then his aunt's question about a flat and a wife made him feel time was running out.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling on the train home?
qa.a: He felt small and left behind as he scrolled through lives that were not his.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do about this pressure?
qa.a: He could remember that these timelines are not a real deadline, talk to someone he trusts about what he wants, and sort out which things he can still change.

grounding: Shows early regret at 25: comparison shock at a reunion, counting the roads not taken, and the social clock making normal variation feel like failure.

passage:
At two in the morning Rajni drafted a resignation letter. Then she opened a travel site and checked one-way tickets to Bengaluru, and hovered over a message that would end things with her boyfriend. None of it was decided; it was simply the urge for something to change tonight. On a call, her sister Preeti told her, "Don't send any of it tonight."

Instead she took a notebook and split a page in two. Left side: what she could still fix, such as learning to code in the evenings, asking for another team, mending an old friendship. Right side: what was gone, like the year after college and the course she had never done. Then she wrote what she truly valued: making things with her hands, working with people she liked, and the city she loved. It was a direction, not a dread.

So she tried small things. She took a weekend design course, started a side project redesigning the neighbourhood library's posters, and had coffee with Nikita, who worked in design. "It's slow at first, and the pay was worse," Nikita said. "I'd do it again." Rajni learned more from those three things than from six months of dreading.

qa.q: What did Rajni draft at two in the morning?
qa.a: She drafted a resignation letter.

qa.q: How did sorting her regrets and values turn the drastic thoughts into small experiments?
qa.a: The urge to resign, move and end things was a signal, but Rajni split what she could fix from what was gone and wrote what she valued, which pointed toward design. A weekend course, a poster project and coffee with Nikita then tested it cheaply without burning bridges.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling while drafting the letter?
qa.a: She felt restless and dissatisfied, wanting something to change overnight.

qa.q: What could Rajni do if the course goes well?
qa.a: She could keep the experiments small, ask Nikita for feedback, and make bigger changes only after real feedback.

grounding: Shows the middle of regret at 25: restless drastic thoughts, sorting regret from values, and small cheap experiments toward a new direction.

passage:
By March, Zeenat's headaches arrived on Sunday afternoons like clockwork. Her stomach knotted at the thought of Monday. At home she snapped at Irawati over a wet towel and then apologised, confused by her own anger. She kept telling herself she just needed to toughen up.

On the third Monday of the release crunch she did not get out of bed. The alarm rang; she watched the ceiling; she could not lift her arm to turn it off. She slept through most of the weekend and woke up feeling worse. She thought, I have failed. Irawati sat on the edge of the bed. "Your body stopped the schedule for you."

That afternoon she emailed Tenzin, her manager, and told him the truth: how many tasks she carried, and that she was not sleeping. She handed two modules to a colleague and asked to skip the on-call week. Tenzin replied within the hour. "Thank you for telling me. Let's redo the plan on Wednesday." Zeenat began eating lunch away from her desk and put her phone in another room at night.

qa.q: What did Zeenat hand to a colleague?
qa.a: She handed two modules to a colleague.

qa.q: How did the early body signals, the collapse and Zeenat's honest email fit together?
qa.a: The Sunday headaches, the knotted stomach and snapping at Irawati were alarms she ignored until the Monday she could not get up. The crash forced the rest, and telling Tenzin the truth about her load led to handing off modules and protecting sleep and meals, while Tenzin adjusted the plan instead of blaming her.

qa.q: What was Zeenat thinking when she could not get out of bed?
qa.a: She thought she had failed, though Irawati saw her body stopping the schedule for her.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do next to support Zeenat?
qa.a: He could redo the plan with her, keep an eye on her load, and check in regularly about workload and sleep.

grounding: Shows the later stages of burnout: body and mood as alarms, a collapse, and honest talk with a manager leading to boundaries.

passage:
At every family dinner Joseph seemed to mention a cousin: Ashwin was at a bank now, Divya had won a scholarship. Chetan's sketchbooks, when he showed them, earned a glance and "that's a hobby." Over the years he began to believe there was nothing he could show that would please his father as he was.

The night he switched his course from engineering to fine arts, the shouting bounced off the walls. "You'll be begging for a job." "You never once looked at what I make!" Chetan packed a bag and left for a friend's flat. "Don't call me," he said at the door. Half of him felt light. Half of him was terrified. Pride made the decision feel welded shut.

In the months after, he told Vikas, and everyone else, the same simple story: his father was a tyrant who cared only about marks. Joseph told the men at his office that his son had thrown away everything they had given him. Chetan could no longer quite recall the Sunday his father had taught him to ride a bicycle, one hand steady on the seat. The man on the other side had become a shape, and a shape was easy to stay angry at.

qa.q: What did Joseph say about Chetan's sketchbooks?
qa.a: He called them a hobby.

qa.q: How did the years of comparisons lead to the rupture and then to the hardened stories?
qa.a: Years of cousin comparisons and "that's a hobby" built Chetan's belief that he could not be accepted, so the argument over his course ended with him leaving. Afterwards each side told a simple villain story, and Chetan lost the memory of his father steadying the bicycle.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel as he left with his bag?
qa.a: He felt light and terrified at once, and pride made the decision feel final.

qa.q: What could Chetan do to keep the door from welding shut?
qa.a: He could hold on to the tender memories, tell a trusted friend or relative that he misses his father, and avoid the simple villain story.

grounding: Shows the early stages of a father-son estrangement: years of accumulated hurt, a rupture over the course, and both sides hardening their stories.

passage:
Wasim told anyone who asked that his son was ungrateful. Yet the room at the end of the corridor still had its bed made and Abhinav's cricket poster on the wall, and late at night Wasim scrolled through his son's public photos with the screen dimmed, in case anyone walked in. He mistook waiting for dignity.

Abhinav's aunt Salma, Wasim's sister, drank tea at Wasim's house one Sunday and said nothing about any of it. At Abhinav's flat the following week she said, casually, "Your father still keeps your room the way you left it. He reads your posts. He won't say." Abhinav's jaw worked. "He called me ungrateful." "Mm," said Salma, and moved on to the samosas. To Wasim she said, "He asks about your knee. He'd like to hear your voice." Neither man said yes or no.

Three weeks later, Abhinav texted a café address. They sat with tea between them. "Not the course today," Abhinav said. "Agreed," said Wasim, gripping the cup. Each said one true thing: "I missed you," from the father; "I was afraid you'd never accept me," from the son. They paid, walked out, and stood on the pavement for a moment, agreeing on nothing, and not needing to.

qa.q: What was still on the wall of Abhinav's old room?
qa.a: Abhinav's cricket poster was still on the wall.

qa.q: How did Salma's messages and the café meeting reflect the pride on both sides?
qa.a: Wasim mistook waiting for dignity and Abhinav clung to being called ungrateful, so neither could reach out. Salma carried each one's softness without pushing, and the café meeting worked because they set the course aside and each said one true thing.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel scrolling through his son's photos at night?
qa.a: He felt hurt and longing, hidden behind pride, which is why he dimmed the screen.

qa.q: What could Wasim and Abhinav do after the first meeting?
qa.a: They could meet again briefly, keep the course topic for later, and let closeness grow without needing full agreement.

grounding: Shows the later stages of a father-son estrangement: a parent's silent grief, an aunt carrying softness between them, and a small first meeting.

passage:
Ira held up her phone. "Swati's birthday party is on Saturday. It ends at eleven, Mum." Zeenat kept stirring the pot. "No. Too late." "Everyone's going." "I said no." Ira felt her growing independence not seen at all, as if she were still ten. What Zeenat could not say aloud was that she pictured dark roads and an auto she could not track, and herself being the one responsible if anything went wrong.

"Because I said so," Zeenat said, sharper than she meant. "You never trust me," Ira shot back. Each heard disrespect. Neither said what sat underneath: I am worried, and I want you to believe in me.

The voices rose. "Last month you lied about the library," Zeenat said. "And your marks are slipping too." "Oh, so now we're doing my whole life," Ira said, with a small laugh that had no laughter in it. Zeenat launched into a lecture about friends who lead you astray. The party dissolved somewhere in the steam from the pot, and neither could quite remember what the fight was about.

qa.q: When did the party end?
qa.a: It ended at eleven.

qa.q: How did what Zeenat could not say aloud differ from what she actually said, and how did that lead to old material coming in?
qa.a: Zeenat's real feeling was worry about dark roads and being responsible, but it came out as "Because I said so." Ira heard disrespect and felt unseen, and as the voices rose old failures like the library lie and her marks were dragged in, so the party was lost.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Zeenat said no?
qa.a: She felt unseen and frustrated, as if her growing independence were being ignored.

qa.q: What could Zeenat do to reset the conversation?
qa.a: She could name her worry aloud and ask what would make the evening safe, such as a ride home and a check-in text.

grounding: Shows the start of a parent-teen conflict cycle: a rule meeting a growing self, command and protest with unspoken feelings, and escalation with old material.
